title: Integer factorization in randomized polynomial time
formal: Do there exist constants C,c and a uniform classical randomized algorithm that, on every positive integer N given in binary, outputs its complete prime factorization with probability at least \(2/3\) and always halts within \(C(n+1)^{c}\) bit operations, where \(n=\lfloor \log _{2}N\rfloor +1\)?
definitions: For \(N\ge 2\), the required output is the ordered list \((p_{1},e_{1}),\ldots ,(p_{r},e_{r})\), with distinct primes \(p_{1}<\cdots <p_{r}\), positive integer exponents \(e_{i}\), and \(N=\prod _{i}p_{i}^{e_{i}}\). All output integers are encoded in binary. The factorization of \(N=1\) is the empty list; zero and malformed encodings are outside the positive-integer domain and are rejected. The same finite probabilistic Turing machine must work for all N. Its random tape contains independent fair bits, and the success probability is over these bits separately for each fixed input. The polynomial time bound holds on every random tape. An incorrect output or a failure symbol counts as failure. There are no quantum operations, input-dependent advice, factoring or order-finding oracles, promises of a special form for N, or supplied factors of nearby integers. In particular n is the bit length of N, not its numerical value.
answer_criterion: Answer yes with a proved algorithm meeting the worst-case polynomial running time and per-input success guarantee. Answer no by proving that every uniform classical randomized algorithm fails one of these requirements for some inputs, regardless of its polynomial exponent. Deterministic factoring would suffice for yes, but a deterministic lower bound alone would not suffice for no. Experiments or algorithms for a restricted class of integers do not settle the statement.
why: Integer factorization is a basic inverse problem in arithmetic and a central test case for the potential power of quantum computation. Its classical complexity has direct consequences for factoring-based cryptography and for algorithms that currently require access to a factoring subroutine.

importance.reason: A defining open problem of computational number theory, with broad consequences for cryptography, arithmetic algorithms, and classical-versus-quantum computation.

progress.text: Sieve methods establish powerful subexponential classical approaches. The standard general number field sieve estimate remains a heuristic expected-time analysis, as summarized in the current large-order paper.
Shor gives polynomial-time quantum algorithms for factorization and discrete logarithms. Quantum computation is outside the classical model fixed here.
Agrawal, Kayal, and Saxena prove deterministic polynomial-time primality testing. The result does not give a polynomial-time factoring algorithm.
Harvey and Hittmeir rigorously factor N in \(O(N^{1/5}(\log  N)^{16/5}/(\log  \log  N)^{3/5})\) deterministic bit operations, improving the preceding exponent-one-fifth bound by a logarithmic factor.

Harvey and Hittmeir’s revised large-order algorithm removes earlier power-of-N lower restrictions on its target order parameter. Their introduction still explicitly identifies polynomial-time integer factorization as unknown; the improved subroutine does not provide such a factoring algorithm.

status_note: Explicitly identified as unknown in Harvey and Hittmeir’s June 2026 paper. Research through 10 September 2026 found no proved classical polynomial-time algorithm for all integers or impossibility theorem for the stated randomized model. Numerical scaling evidence and quantum algorithms do not establish either answer.

context_blocks.text: Multiplying the prime factors is easy, and the factors themselves fit in a polynomial-size output. Discovering them is the unresolved step. Trial division up to \(\sqrt{N}\) is polynomial in the number’s value but exponential in its binary input length. The distinction between N and log N is essential even when a newer algorithm improves the power of N substantially.

Primality testing and factorization are different tasks. The Agrawal–Kayal–Saxena algorithm decides in deterministic polynomial time whether a number is prime, without necessarily exhibiting a divisor when the answer is composite. It also makes a proposed full factorization efficiently checkable: verify that every listed base is prime and that the product is N.

Because an output can be checked, a bounded-error polynomial-time factoring algorithm can be repeated until a valid factorization is obtained, giving an always-correct algorithm with polynomial expected time. Conversely, a polynomial expected-time always-correct algorithm can be truncated at a suitable constant multiple of its expected bound to obtain the formulation above. This equivalence concerns performance on every input; success on a sampled family of integers alone is weaker.

The general number field sieve has the familiar heuristic expected-time estimate \(\exp (((64/9)^{1/3}+o(1))(\ln  N)^{1/3}(\ln  \ln  N)^{2/3})\). This is subexponential but still superpolynomial in the bit length. Rigorous deterministic bounds of \(N^{1/5+o(1)}\) make a different tradeoff and remain exponential in that length. Neither bound is a proof that faster classical factoring is impossible.

Shor’s quantum algorithm factors in polynomial time, using quantum order finding. It provides an upper bound in a more powerful computational model; it does not establish a classical lower bound. A classical polynomial-time algorithm would undermine factoring-based cryptographic assumptions, but the absence of such an algorithm has not been proved from \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) or from the efficiency of multiplication.

sentences: Integer factorization recovers the prime factors and multiplicities whose product is a given positive integer.
The reviewed question asks whether one classical randomized algorithm can do this in time polynomial in the input's bit length.
Multiplication and verification are efficient, but discovering factors remains a different computational task from testing primality.
A polynomial algorithm would transform computational number theory and undermine corresponding factoring-based hardness assumptions.
The saved review distinguishes subexponential classical methods and polynomial-time quantum factoring from the requested worst-case classical guarantee on every input.
